title: Version control with git

read.title: Branches are just pointers
text: Git does not store a project as a pile of diffs. Each commit is a snapshot of every tracked file, plus the author, a message, and pointers to its parent commits. Git names each commit by a hash of its contents, so changing anything in history produces new commits with new names.

A branch is nothing more than a movable pointer to one commit, which is why creating a branch is instant. HEAD records which branch you are on, and every new commit moves that branch forward. When you merge a branch that is strictly ahead of yours, Git can fast-forward, simply sliding the pointer. When the two lines have diverged, Git performs a three-way merge using both tips and their common ancestor and records a merge commit.

Rebasing reaches the same final code by a different route. It takes your commits, replays them one at a time on top of another branch, and moves your branch to the result, giving a straight-line history. Because the replayed commits are new objects, rebasing commits that other people already have forces them to untangle duplicates. Pro Git's rule is simple: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.

q.q: Why is creating a branch in Git instant?
o: Git copies files in the background
A branch is only a pointer to a commit

q.q: When can Git fast-forward a merge?
o: When the merged branch is strictly ahead of yours
When there are no files changed

q.q: Why is rebasing shared commits risky?
o: Rebase only works on the main branch
Replayed commits are new objects, so collaborators get duplicates
